Taxi's behaving badly

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The taxi business is the biggest commuter transporter in the country, transporting 65 -70% of the country's workforce on any given day, but it’s also one of the most lawless and dangerous industries

Summary:
It's estimated that over 1000 deaths are recorded on South african roads every month and "the popular belief is that taxi drivers’ behaviour – their aggressive driving and disdain for the rules – provides an intuitive and logical explanation for why South Africa’s roads are so dangerous."

In September this year, Carte Blanche put out a social media call out to our viewers for pictures and footage of 'taxi's behaving badly badly'. We received a massive response with a reach of between 400 000 and 500 000 viewers either commenting on their experiences with taxi's on the road as well as hundreds of pictures and videos of the various incidents'. At face value, many of the videos and pictures that we were sent, confirm this belief. Statistics too from confirm that taxis "account for three times more fatalities than cars".

But taxi drivers say that's not the full story. They face major pressures both from commuters to get them to their destinantions on time and from their bosses to make sure that the routes they operate on are profitable.

In this insert we will film reality style with a taxi driver and he takes us through the ins and outs of the taxi business. We will also speak to one of the biggest Taxi unions in the country, along with commuters and taxi bosses.

We have accident footage from ER24 that we can also use.

This week, Carte Blanche takes the taxi industry to task and finds out who's responsible to put an end to the carnage and lawlessness caused by taxi drivers on our roads.




Further information:
We will also get an inside look at this booming industry, the pressures that drivers and operators face and why they will do anything - including risk the lives of commuters and fellow drivers - to get to their destinations first.

We have a taxi driver and taxi owner who have agreed to talk to us and to take us along on one of their routes.

With the assistance of the JMPD, we will be able to film police as they crack down on unlawful and unroadworthy taxi's and taxi drivers.

Extra Budget Items:
As part of our filming, the entire crew (presenter, camera and producer) will have to take a few taxi's along the route, so we will need taxi fare for at least one day's shoot.

An average taxi route costs about R10per person, single trip.

Press Release:


Taxis Behaving Badly
They’ve plugged the void in South Africa’s public transport market. But does this justify their often lawless and dangerous behaviour on our roads? Dealing with congested routes and hot-headed motorists, Carte Blanche goes behind the wheel with the drivers who move over 65 percent of our nation, to experience the cut throat taxi industry first-hand.


Script:


Script
Visual on screen

VO: It’s peak hour traffic... Thousands of drivers descend on the roads, filling up highways and clogging back routes.

Here, it’s not uncommon to see taxis skipping red traffic lights, driving on the wrong side of the road towards oncoming cars, or just using the lanes intended for emergency vehicles - all in an effort to beat traffic.

This is where angry motorists and aggravated taxi drivers come head to head.
Open with drone sequence
UPSOUND 49:52- Gert: I’ve seen quite a few near misses, serious head-on collisions, I’ve seen little bumper bashes, a lot of them.

VO: Over the past few months, Carte Blanche has received some startling footage from our viewers.

From a taxi ramping an island to switch direction, to an off-the-road police chase as a driver tries to evade officials.

And this was just the tip of the iceberg.



Bring in viewer submissions\write to visuals
VO: Gert Fourie is a former police officer and he used to spend many mornings filming taxi drivers as they broke road regulations in the main road close to his home in Pretoria.

UPSOUND 45:36 - Gert: I’ve been doing this for 5 years ... from 6 to 8 I was down at the bottom. Car in the middle of the road, Video camera up taking footage and it was shared with RTMC, Metro, and still the problem is going on.

UPSOUND Fatima Kgomo: They stop wherever a person says hey short left; they have to stop because that’s where I want to get off, that’s where you want to get off... They’re just doing their job.

VO: They’ve plugged the void in South Africa’s public transport market. But does this justify their lawless and dangerous behaviour on our roads?

Fatima Kgomo only recently bought her car and before that, she says, taxis were her only mode of transport.

UPSOUND Fatima: They’re very crucial especially in the majority of black communities because a lot of people don’t have cars or cannot drive or cannot afford to get a car.

VO: But while driving a taxi full of commuters, many taxi drivers risk the lives of their passengers with their often careless disregard for simple road rules.

LINK: And it’s in the peak of traffic that we see the most dangerous and irresponsible driving, really putting lives at risk...look at this.

DEREK – Gert, surely these drivers have a job to do; they’ve got to get their passengers to work on time.

UPSOUND 47:43- Gert: A job to do compared to blatantly breaking the law, ignoring traffic rules and endangering other road users' lives... it’s just not on.

VO: It’s a highly organised industry, with all taxi owners belonging to an operating body known as an association.

There are around 2000 associations which monitor all the routes for the 200 000 taxis on our roads.

These taxis transport a large majority of the country’s commuting workforce.

UPSOUND TCR NTA Alpheus Mlalazi: Percentage-wise it’s between 65 and 76% but in figures, it’s between 15 and 16 million commuters per day.
VO: Alpheus Mlalazi is the spokesperson of the National taxi Alliance and he believes that without the taxi industry, South Africa’s economy would be brought to its knees.

UPSOUND Alpheus: Between 65 and 75% of the commuting public depends on taxis to go to work and whatever they want to do. If we take that away from them, really we are depriving them of their economic freedom right.

UPSOUND MEC Ismail Vadi :
... There’s no doubt if the taxi services are withdrawn, on any work day in this province it will have an impact on our economic performance for that period.

VO: Ismail Vadi, the Gauteng MEC for Road and Transport, believes that the taxi industry is an important part of the public transport system, especially for his province.

UPSOUND MEC Ismail Vadi:
They are an essential ingredient, essential component of the public transport system.

They move large numbers of people, largely for daily commuting and then sometimes for recreational purposes.

LINK: This is Diepsloot, quite a long way North of Joburg, and every week day thousands of commuters, have to take taxis to Sandton, Randburg, Hillbrow or even the City.
Drone footage of Diepsloot
VO: Anita Moyo is from Diepsloot and every day she takes taxis to Rosebank or Hyde Park, where she works part-time as a domestic worker.

She says that taking taxis is a necessity.

UPSOUND Anita: We definitely need them....They are the ones that take us to work. We don’t have cars, so we need to use them.
UPSOUND Anita: If there were buses, I would use them because they are cheap and safe most of the times, but there are no buses here in Diepsloot that’s why I use the taxi.

VO: Anita says she has often been in taxis, where the drivers break traffic rules.

UPSOUND Anita: Some of them skip robots, they skip them when they’re closed.??
Most of the times I keep quiet, you just look because you’re scared. Sometimes, they will tell you to get out the taxi then you will be late for work.


VO: We decided to hop onto a taxi from Diepsloot.
On the way, we spoke to Kate who was heading to work.
She says often, it’s the passengers, who push the drivers to break regulations.

Sequence of Derek in the taxi...
UPSOUND KATE - TCR: 12:44:15:24
... Especially when there is traffic, they’ll just tell them “no, you can’t keep following the traffic” can you please keep to the side pocket... they call the yellow lines side pocket... They do encourage them to break the traffic law.

VO: Stoffel Holthausen is one of about 21000 traffic
officials that we have on our roads and his motorbike is kitted
out with a number of cameras. He also sent us some footage
that he’s been filming.

Bring in Stoffel footage.
DEREK: When it comes to taxis on our roads, Stoffel, what
are you seeing?

UPSOUND Stoffel 03:13 -03:28 ... there is a lot of them ....that don't abide to the road traffic acts and because most of them are getting away with it... there’s some of the normal public are doing the same now.

VO: And sometimes, careless disregard for traffic laws can have devastating consequences.

LINK Derek: Most taxis carry 15 passengers or more and wearing a seat belt is a rarity, so you can imagine in the event of an accident, it can have really tragic consequences.

UPSOUND Fatima: It’s just hell. I’ve been in a taxi accident, so after that accident it was kind of hard for me to get back into a taxi.

VO: Advocate Makhosini Msibi is the CEO of the Road Traffic Management Corporation and he says that when it comes to road traffic accidents, taxi drivers aren’t always to blame.

UPSOUND Advocate Msibi TCR: 13:37:57:00 - Informed by statistics, taxis are just about the 10% contributor to our national pandemonium problems that we are confronting in terms of fatalities. … 45% of fatalities arises from the private owners of these small motor vehicles, so we are also a problem.




VO: But with over 11 million vehicles on our roads and only 200 000 taxis it would seem that even 10% is too high.

LINK: We spend a lot of time complaining about taxi drivers, maybe fuming is a better word, but what’s it like behind their steering wheel.

VO: We hit the streets to find out from taxi drivers what’s behind their reckless driving.

‘UPSOUND Peter: Look I’m carrying 15 people there, the other person is carrying 15... We are under pressure from them too. They saying Mr Driver we are getting late. So I must make some means.


UPSOUND TCR: 14:05:08:06 - Erustos: You drivers you
drive like somehow, you put us in an awkward situation
somehow because you find the robot is caution and then I
have to drop people at work and then, you want to stop at
the robot, so what must I do?

VO: Erustos admits it’s literally a race against time.
Time lapse
UPSOUND TCR: 14:05:08:06 Erustos - I am running after
time. I must make money, I must take people to work, and
then wena you wannna stop at the robot, you wanna the
Regulations and the rules.

UPSOUND TCR: 13:52:08:00
Peter: The most important thing is time, because these people are not going to one place, they go to work, they go to different places.

VO: During peak traffic, a taxi driver has to make at least five
return trips on their route so that they make enough
money for both the owners and themselves.

UPSOUND TCR: 14:07:21:02 Erustos: I earn my money
weekly, so daily I have a limit that I must make. ... So during
the day, I must make sure that I reach that target.

VO: So to reach what would look like an impossible target,
sometimes taxi drivers will do whatever it takes.

UPSOUND TCR: 13:04:29:07 Lorraine: I admit to that. We have a problem and we are still fixing up that problem.

VO: Lorraine Sifuba is one of only a few women who are taxi owners. She says that owners are concerned with the way some taxi drivers behave, but there is always recourse for disgruntled motorists.

UPSOUND: TCR: 13:03:26:09 Lorraine: We have an association first... If the driver has done something wrong on the road, the person that has been wronged must go to the office; you just take a number plate... they discipline the driver for the wrongs that he did on the road.

VO: And for many in the taxi industry, it would seem there is an easy solution.

UPSOUND Lorraine Sifuba - TCR: 13:06:37:00
We’ve been asking the government – make dedicated lanes for the taxis... instead, it’s the buses.

UPSOUND Alpheus Mlalazi - TCR: 14:02:16:01
... Every time, the NTA... we’ve gone to government to say we need dedicated public lanes so that we can move people that are really driving the economy, we are told that there isn’t enough space


UPSOUND Msibi - TCR: 13:44:01
Well the lanes that are specialised are for buses for rapid bus transit. .. We don’t believe that we can then have dedicated lanes for taxi operators.

UPSOUND MEC Vadi: We just don’t have the road reserves and the space and money to build more and more roads. So the only answer we have is to build the public transport system.

VO: But Vadi believes that it’s only a matter of time before
government brings the taxi industry under control.

UPSOUND MEC Vadi:
We are beginning to take action, so there is a concerted effort.
Now, are we there? No. We are not there, but it doesn’t mean
we are giving up.

VO: We hit the streets to find out from taxi drivers what’s behind their reckless driving. ‘UPSOUND Peter: Look I’m carrying 15 people there, the other person is carrying 15... We are under pressure from them too. They saying Mr Driver we are getting late. So I must make some means. UPSOUND TCR: 14:05:08:06 - Erustos: You drivers you drive like somehow, you put us in an awkward situation somehow because you find the robot is caution and then I have to drop people at work and then, you want to stop at the robot, so what must I do? VO: Erustos admits it’s literally a race against time. Time lapse UPSOUND TCR: 14:05:08:06 Erustos - I am running after time. I must make money, I must take people to work, and then wena you wannna stop at the robot, you wanna the Regulations and the rules. UPSOUND TCR: 13:52:08:00 Peter: The most important thing is time, because these people are not going to one place, they go to work, they go to different places. VO: During peak traffic, a taxi driver has to make at least five return trips on their route so that they make enough money for both the owners and themselves. UPSOUND TCR: 14:07:21:02 Erustos: I earn my money weekly, so daily I have a limit that I must make. ... So during the day, I must make sure that I reach that target. VO: So to reach what would look like an impossible target, sometimes taxi drivers will do whatever it takes. UPSOUND TCR: 13:04:29:07 Lorraine: I admit to that. We have a problem and we are still fixing up that problem. VO: Lorraine Sifuba is one of only a few women who are taxi owners. She says that owners are concerned with the way some taxi drivers behave, but there is always recourse for disgruntled motorists. UPSOUND: TCR: 13:03:26:09 Lorraine: We have an association first... If the driver has done something wrong on the road, the person that has been wronged must go to the office; you just take a number plate... they discipline the driver for the wrongs that he did on the road. VO: And for many in the taxi industry, it would seem there is an easy solution. UPSOUND Lorraine Sifuba - TCR: 13:06:37:00 We’ve been asking the government – make dedicated lanes for the taxis... instead, it’s the buses. UPSOUND Alpheus Mlalazi - TCR: 14:02:16:01 ... Every time, the NTA... we’ve gone to government to say we need dedicated public lanes so that we can move people that are really driving the economy, we are told that there isn’t enough space UPSOUND Msibi - TCR: 13:44:01 Well the lanes that are specialised are for buses for rapid bus transit. .. We don’t believe that we can then have dedicated lanes for taxi operators. UPSOUND MEC Vadi: We just don’t have the road reserves and the space and money to build more and more roads. So the only answer we have is to build the public transport system. VO: But Vadi believes that it’s only a matter of time before government brings the taxi industry under control. UPSOUND MEC Vadi: We are beginning to take action, so there is a concerted effort. Now, are we there? No. We are not there, but it doesn’t mean we are giving up.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The taxi business is the biggest commuter transporter in the country, transporting 65 -70% of the country's workforce on any given day, but it’s also one of the most lawless and dangerous industries
metadata.Summary: It's estimated that over 1000 deaths are recorded on South african roads every month and "the popular belief is that taxi drivers’ behaviour – their aggressive driving and disdain for the rules – provides an intuitive and logical explanation for why South Africa’s roads are so dangerous." In September this year, Carte Blanche put out a social media call out to our viewers for pictures and footage of 'taxi's behaving badly badly'. We received a massive response with a reach of between 400 000 and 500 000 viewers either commenting on their experiences with taxi's on the road as well as hundreds of pictures and videos of the various incidents'. At face value, many of the videos and pictures that we were sent, confirm this belief. Statistics too from confirm that taxis "account for three times more fatalities than cars". But taxi drivers say that's not the full story. They face major pressures both from commuters to get them to their destinantions on time and from their bosses to make sure that the routes they operate on are profitable. In this insert we will film reality style with a taxi driver and he takes us through the ins and outs of the taxi business. We will also speak to one of the biggest Taxi unions in the country, along with commuters and taxi bosses. We have accident footage from ER24 that we can also use. This week, Carte Blanche takes the taxi industry to task and finds out who's responsible to put an end to the carnage and lawlessness caused by taxi drivers on our roads.
metadata.Further information: We will also get an inside look at this booming industry, the pressures that drivers and operators face and why they will do anything - including risk the lives of commuters and fellow drivers - to get to their destinations first. We have a taxi driver and taxi owner who have agreed to talk to us and to take us along on one of their routes. With the assistance of the JMPD, we will be able to film police as they crack down on unlawful and unroadworthy taxi's and taxi drivers.
metadata.Extra Budget Items: As part of our filming, the entire crew (presenter, camera and producer) will have to take a few taxi's along the route, so we will need taxi fare for at least one day's shoot. An average taxi route costs about R10per person, single trip.
